interactions.label: Which artery's occlusion would most likely cause contralateral face and arm weak

params.question: Which artery's occlusion would most likely cause contralateral face and arm weakness along with aphasia?

answers.text: Posterior cerebral artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The PCA supplies the occipital lobes. Its strokes characteristically produce contralateral homonymous hemianopia, not motor weakness or aphasia.

answers.text: Anterior cerebral artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The ACA supplies the medial surface of the hemisphere. Its strokes typically produce leg-dominant weakness with relative sparing of the face and arm.

answers.text: Middle cerebral artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The MCA supplies the lateral cortex, including motor, sensory, and language areas. Its occlusion causes contralateral face and arm weakness, and aphasia when the dominant hemisphere is involved.

answers.text: Basilar artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The basilar artery supplies the brainstem and cerebellum. Its occlusion produces posterior circulation signs such as vertigo, ataxia, and cranial nerve palsies rather than cortical motor deficits.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the vascular territories: the MCA covers the lateral cortex (motor, sensory, language areas), while the ACA covers medial surfaces and the PCA covers the occipital lobes.
Correct. The MCA is the most commonly affected artery in stroke, and its lateral cortical territory explains the classic triad of face–arm hemiplegia with aphasia.

params.question: A patient is found with left-sided weakness upon waking at 6:00 AM. His wife confirms he was entirely normal when he fell asleep at 11:00 PM. What time determines the start of the thrombolysis window?

answers.text: 6:00 AM, when the deficit was first noticed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In wake-up strokes the actual onset is unknown. Using the time of discovery would overestimate the available window and risk treating outside the safe period.

answers.text: 12:00 AM, as a reasonable midpoint estimate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Midpoint estimation is not standard practice. The last-known-well time provides a definite, reproducible reference point for the treatment decision.

answers.text: The time of arrival in the emergency department

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The thrombolysis window is calculated from symptom onset or last-known-well time, not from hospital arrival. Door-to-needle time is a separate quality metric.

answers.text: 11:00 PM, the last time he was known to be well

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In wake-up strokes the last-known-well time — when the patient fell asleep symptom-free — is used as the conservative onset marker for thrombolysis eligibility.

overallFeedback.feedback: In wake-up strokes, always ask: 'When was the patient last known to be well?' That time — when he fell asleep normal — starts the thrombolysis clock, not when the deficit was discovered.
Correct. The last-known-well time is the standard for calculating the thrombolysis window in wake-up strokes, ensuring treatment stays within the safe period.

interactions.label: A patient presents with sudden-onset hemiplegia of unknown onset time. MRI shows

params.question: A patient presents with sudden-onset hemiplegia of unknown onset time. MRI shows a bright lesion on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) but no corresponding signal on FLAIR. What does this mismatch indicate?

answers.text: The stroke occurred more than 24 hours ago

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In older strokes FLAIR signal appears alongside DWI changes. The absence of FLAIR signal indicates the stroke is recent, not old.

answers.text: The stroke is likely less than 4.5 hours old, supporting thrombolysis eligibility

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DWI-FLAIR mismatch indicates the ischaemic event occurred recently — under approximately 4.5 hours — allowing thrombolysis even when onset time is unknown, as in wake-up strokes.

answers.text: The lesion is haemorrhagic rather than ischaemic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DWI positivity with FLAIR negativity is a hallmark of acute ischaemic stroke. Haemorrhage has a distinct appearance on these MRI sequences.

answers.text: The imaging findings are artefactual and the scan should be repeated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DWI-FLAIR mismatch is a well-validated imaging sign used routinely in clinical stroke evaluation. It is not artefactual.

overallFeedback.feedback: DWI lights up within minutes of ischaemia. FLAIR takes longer to become positive. When DWI is bright but FLAIR is dark, the stroke is recent — likely under 4.5 hours — and thrombolysis can be considered.
Correct. DWI-FLAIR mismatch is a validated imaging surrogate for recent stroke onset, guiding thrombolysis decisions when the exact onset time is unknown.

interactions.label: A 65-year-old patient with acute ischaemic stroke presents within 3 hours of ons

params.question: A 65-year-old patient with acute ischaemic stroke presents within 3 hours of onset. His blood pressure is 192/114 mmHg and he is otherwise eligible for thrombolysis. What is the correct next step?

answers.text: Lower the blood pressure to below 185/110 mmHg with intravenous labetalol, then administer alteplase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blood pressure must be below 185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis can be given. This threshold is distinct from the permissive 220/120 mmHg target used when thrombolysis is withheld.

answers.text: Administer alteplase immediately, as the blood pressure is acceptable for thrombolysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At 192/114 the blood pressure exceeds the 185/110 mmHg threshold for thrombolysis. Administering the drug at this level increases the risk of haemorrhagic transformation.

answers.text: Allow permissive hypertension up to 220/120 mmHg and proceed with thrombolysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 220/120 mmHg threshold applies only when thrombolysis is NOT being given. Thrombolysis candidates must meet the stricter limit of 185/110 mmHg first.

answers.text: Withhold thrombolysis permanently, as this blood pressure is an absolute contraindication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Elevated blood pressure is a relative, not absolute, contraindication. If safely lowered to below 185/110, thrombolysis can proceed. The four absolute stops are haemorrhage on scan, active bleeding, recent surgery, and INR above 1.7.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the two distinct BP thresholds: below 185/110 mmHg is required BEFORE giving thrombolysis; the more permissive 220/120 applies only when thrombolysis is not being administered.
Correct. The two BP thresholds — 185/110 for thrombolysis candidates and 220/120 when thrombolysis is withheld — are a frequent source of clinical error.

interactions.label: Mr Pillai is three weeks post left MCA stroke with right hemiplegia and Broca's

params.question: Mr Pillai is three weeks post left MCA stroke with right hemiplegia and Broca's aphasia. His wife is considering a care home. Beyond addressing her immediate questions, which often-overlooked area should you proactively discuss before discharge?

answers.text: The precise date by which full neurological recovery will occur

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: False precision in prognosis damages trust when reality diverges from the prediction. The skill is communicating genuine uncertainty while providing a framework for planning.

answers.text: Caregiver burnout and the need for support

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Unrecognised caregiver burnout is one of the most common reasons home rehabilitation fails. Acknowledging the caregiver's needs directly and discussing support resources is essential at every post-stroke family meeting.

answers.text: Genetic counselling for stroke predisposition in family members

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While family history is a risk factor, routine genetic counselling is not part of standard post-stroke discharge counselling for a hypertensive stroke patient.

answers.text: Immediate return-to-work clearance to maintain financial stability

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Return to work should be discussed at discharge, but it requires staged planning and occupational assessment — not immediate clearance at three weeks post-stroke.

overallFeedback.feedback: The narration identifies caregiver burnout as one of the most common reasons home rehabilitation fails. Acknowledging the caregiver directly — discussing their wellbeing and support needs — should be part of every post-stroke family meeting.
Correct. Caregiver burnout is frequently unrecognised and is a leading reason home-based rehabilitation breaks down. Addressing it proactively supports both the patient and the family.
